updates.summary: Statement of the AI Action Summit in Paris that sets six priorities: accessible AI to reduce digital divides; AI that is open, inclusive, transparent, ethical, safe, secure and trustworthy; innovation without market concentration; AI that shapes work and labour markets positively; sustainable AI; and international cooperation on governance. It commends the Bletchley and Seoul summits' work on AI safety and notes the voluntary commitments made there, says the signatories will keep addressing AI risks to information integrity and continue work on AI transparency, and reaffirms the commitment to a UN Global Dialogue on AI governance and an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
updates.notes: Published on 11 February 2025, the second day of the AI Action Summit, held in Paris on 10 and 11 February 2025. The signatory list names 63 countries, the African Union Commission and the EU; the United States and the United Kingdom are not on it. A footnote limits the statement to civil applications and use of AI. Founding members launched a Public Interest AI Platform and Incubator under it. The International AI Safety Report 2025 (INT-09) was published ahead of the summit.

updates.title: AI Impact Summit Declaration
updates.summary: Declaration of the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, held after the Bletchley, Seoul and Paris summits. It calls for international cooperation along seven pillars: human capital, access for social empowerment, trustworthiness of AI systems, energy efficiency, AI in science, democratising AI resources, and AI for economic growth and social good. Its secure and trusted AI section calls secure, trustworthy and robust AI foundational to trust and recognises security in AI systems, industry-led voluntary measures, technical solutions and policy frameworks across the AI lifecycle. It notes the voluntary Trusted AI Commons, a platform of technical resources, tools, benchmarks and best practices.
updates.notes: The declaration is headed 'AI Impact Summit Declaration, New Delhi (February 18 - 19, 2026)', and its preamble says the participants gathered in New Delhi on 19 February 2026; the European Commission announced on 20 February 2026 that the EU would endorse it, and the Australian government gives the summit as 19 and 20 February 2026, so only the month is given. The Commission calls it the Leaders' Declaration at the AI Impact Summit, the Australian government the India AI Impact Summit Declaration. The endorsement list published with the text names 89 endorsers: 87 countries, among them the USA, China, India, Russia and the UK, plus the EU and IFAD. Under its pillars the declaration takes note of voluntary deliverables, among them the Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI, the Global AI Impact Commons, the Trusted AI Commons and its guidance note, the International Network of AI for Science Institutions and the Voluntary Guiding Principles on Resilient, Innovative, and Efficient Artificial Intelligence.

updates.summary: Declaration by 28 countries and the EU on the risks of 'frontier' AI: highly capable general-purpose models, and narrow AI with harmful capabilities, that match or exceed today's most advanced models. It warns of substantial risks from intentional misuse or unintended issues of control, names cybersecurity, biotechnology and disinformation, and sees potential for serious, even catastrophic, harm. Its agenda is a shared scientific understanding of these risks and risk-based national policies, with safety testing, evaluations and transparency from developers of frontier AI, and an international network of scientific research on frontier AI safety.
updates.notes: Agreed at the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, 1-2 November 2023; the countries represented include the US, China and the EU. New Zealand joined the commitment on 23 October 2024, and GOV.UK updated the publication on 13 February 2025 to include it as a signatory. The participants said they would meet again in 2024. The International AI Safety Report (interim report INT-08, full report INT-09) was launched at this summit. GOV.UK also offers a Latin American Spanish version of the publication.

updates.summary: Leaders of ten countries and the EU treat AI safety, innovation and inclusivity as inter-related goals and call for interoperable AI governance frameworks, in line with a risk-based approach, for the safe, secure and trustworthy design, development, deployment and use of AI. They support creating or expanding AI safety institutes, research programmes and supervisory bodies and networks between them, welcome the annexed Seoul Statement of Intent on AI safety science, recognise the particular responsibility of organisations developing frontier AI, note the Frontier AI Safety Commitments and back the operationalisation of the Hiroshima Process Code of Conduct.
updates.notes: Agreed at the Leaders' Session of the AI Seoul Summit on 21 May 2024. updates.summary: Leaders of ten countries and the EU affirm international coordination, based on openness, transparency and reciprocity, to advance the science of AI safety, and commend the creation or expansion of publicly backed institutions such as AI Safety Institutes. They intend to foster common scientific understanding, including through assessments such as the International AI Safety Report. Possible steps include sharing information about models' capabilities, limitations and risks, monitoring AI harms and safety incidents, exchanging or jointly creating evaluations and data sets, and shared technical resources. They aim to develop an international network to accelerate AI safety science.

updates.summary: Ministers of 27 countries and the EU recognise their role in establishing frameworks to manage risks from frontier AI models, in promoting credible external evaluations, and in identifying, with the private sector, civil society and academia, thresholds at which unmitigated risks would be severe. Their examples are capabilities that meaningfully assist non-state actors with chemical or biological weapons, and capabilities or propensities to evade human oversight through manipulation, deception or autonomous replication. Through their AI safety institutes they plan to share best practices and evaluation datasets and to collaborate on safety testing guidelines.
updates.notes: Agreed at the Ministers' Session of the AI Seoul Summit on 22 May 2024; the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom were the summit's co-chairs. Signatories include the US, UK, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Türkiye, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda and the EU; China is not on the list. Ministers planned to develop proposals on thresholds and capabilities for consideration before the AI Action Summit in France (INT-01), and looked forward to the final International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI, whose interim report (INT-08) they noted.

updates.summary: Interim edition of the first International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI, written by 75 AI experts with an Expert Advisory Panel nominated by 30 countries, the EU and the UN. It synthesises the evidence on the capabilities of general-purpose AI and sorts its risks into malicious use (fake content, disinformation, cyber offence, biological weapons), malfunctions (bias, loss of control) and systemic risks (labour markets, the AI divide, market concentration, privacy, copyright). It finds that technical methods such as benchmarking, red-teaming and auditing training data can help mitigate risks but all have limitations. It does not discuss policy interventions.
updates.notes: Commissioned at the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park in November 2023 and chaired by Yoshua Bengio, with a UK Government secretariat hosted by the AI Safety Institute; published in May 2024 ahead of the AI Seoul Summit 2024. Executive summaries were published in Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian and Spanish. The interim report said the final version would be published ahead of the AI Action Summit in France; that full report, the International AI Safety Report 2025 (INT-09), followed in January 2025. On 22 October 2025 the GOV.UK page was updated only to add a link to the report's website, internationalaisafetyreport.org.

updates.issuing_body: Independent expert panel chaired by Yoshua Bengio, with a secretariat at the UK AI Safety Institute and Mila – Quebec AI Institute; published by the UK Government (DSIT)
updates.summary: The first full International AI Safety Report, the work of 96 AI experts with an Expert Advisory Panel nominated by 30 countries, the OECD, the EU and the UN. It summarises the scientific evidence on the capabilities of general-purpose AI, including AI agents; on its risks from malicious use (fake content, manipulation, cyber offence, biological and chemical attacks), malfunctions (reliability, bias, loss of control) and systemic effects (labour markets, the AI R&D divide, market concentration, environment, privacy, copyright) and open-weight models; and on technical approaches to identifying, assessing, mitigating and monitoring risks. It does not recommend specific policies.
updates.notes: Published ahead of the AI Action Summit in Paris in February 2025, following the interim report of May 2024 (INT-08), which was presented at the AI Seoul Summit. A Chair's note covers AI advances between the end of the writing period (5 December 2024) and publication, notably early test results of OpenAI's o3 model. The UK Government said it would keep providing the secretariat until a long-term international home was agreed, with Yoshua Bengio as chair for 2025. Two Key Updates followed as separate publications: 'First Key Update: Capabilities and Risk Implications' (15 October 2025) and 'Second Key Update: Technical Safeguards and Risk Management' (25 November 2025). The second edition, the International AI Safety Report 2026 (INT-10), followed on 3 February 2026. The PDF's back page prints the research series number as DSIT 2024/000; its front matter and the website give DSIT 2025/001.

updates.issuing_body: Independent expert panel chaired by Yoshua Bengio, with a secretariat at the UK AI Security Institute and Mila – Quebec AI Institute; published by the UK Government (DSIT)
updates.summary: The second International AI Safety Report, guided by over 100 experts with nominees of over 30 countries and international bodies. It narrows its scope to emerging risks at the frontier of general-purpose AI: malicious use (AI-generated content and crime, manipulation, cyberattacks, biological and chemical weapons), malfunctions (reliability, loss of control) and systemic risks (labour markets, human autonomy). It describes an 'evaluation gap', as pre-deployment tests do not reliably predict real-world risk and models increasingly tell test settings from deployment, and covers defence-in-depth safeguards and Frontier AI Safety Frameworks. It makes no specific policy recommendations.
updates.notes: Published on 3 February 2026 as the second edition of the report series created after the 2023 AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park; the UK minister's foreword says it would be showcased at the India AI Impact Summit. Its scope is narrower than that of the 2025 report (INT-09), which also covered bias, environmental impacts, privacy and copyright, and it is meant to complement the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. It records that in 2025, 12 companies published or updated Frontier AI Safety Frameworks and that most risk-management initiatives remain voluntary, though a few jurisdictions are beginning to make some practices legal requirements. Translations were published in the other five official UN languages, and a 2026 Report: Extended Summary for Policymakers and an Executive Summary were published on the same day.

updates.summary: Mission statement agreed by the ten initial members of the International Network of AI Safety Institutes: Australia, Canada, the EU, France, Japan, Kenya, the Republic of Korea, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States. It sets up the Network as a forum for a common technical understanding of AI safety risks and mitigations that supports interoperable principles and best practices, and names four priority areas: research on the risks and capabilities of advanced AI, common best practices for testing advanced AI systems, which may include joint testing exercises, shared approaches to interpreting tests, and inclusion of countries at all levels of development.
updates.notes: Launched at the Network's inaugural convening in San Francisco, co-hosted by the US Departments of Commerce and State, with the United States as inaugural chair. The US fact sheet released on 20 November 2024 says the ten initial members agreed the joint mission statement ahead of the convening; the statement's own text dates the launch meeting 21 November 2024. The statement builds on the Seoul Statement of Intent of 21 May 2024 (INT-05). At a meeting in San Diego alongside NeurIPS in December 2025, hosted by NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), through which the US takes part, the Network was renamed the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science, and the United Kingdom took on the role of Network Coordinator (announced 9 December 2025). On 13 February 2026 the Network published consensus areas and open questions on practices for automated evaluations. In July 2026, at a meeting in Seoul alongside ICML, it completed its first best-practice guidance document. At their meeting in Paris on 29 May 2026 the G7 digital ministers agreed to start discussions under France's G7 presidency, including members of the Network and the OECD, on the comparability of AI risk-assessment frameworks (G7-04).

updates.summary: Declaration of ministers and high authorities of Latin America and the Caribbean that takes the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI as its reference. It calls for policies, strategies and institutional frameworks for the safe, ethical and responsible design, development and use of AI with a human-rights approach, and the signatories agree to analyse whether new legal frameworks are needed, balancing ex ante regulation of AI risks with innovation. It cites due diligence and impact assessment, human oversight and determination, transparency, monitoring of effects on workers and data governance, and sets up a Chile-led working group towards a regional intergovernmental AI council.
updates.notes: Adopted by the ministers and high authorities meeting in Santiago on 23 and 24 October 2023, at the Forum on the Ethics of AI in Latin America and the Caribbean and the ministerial summit held with it; Chile's Ministry of Science and Ministry of Foreign Affairs prepared the meeting, with technical and financial support from UNESCO and CAF. The text does not list its signatories; InvestChile, Chile's public investment promotion agency, says 20 countries signed it at La Moneda Palace, naming Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, Peru, Paraguay, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, Uruguay and Venezuela. Chile was asked to convene the working group in the first half of 2024. The second summit, in Montevideo on 3 and 4 October 2024, adopted the Declaration of Montevideo (INT-17), which thanks Chile for leading the working group and entrusts Uruguay with continuing its work.

updates.summary: Endorsing states set out measures for the responsible development, deployment and use of military AI, including autonomous functions and systems: use must comply with international law, notably international humanitarian law, and be accountable within a responsible human chain of command and control. Ten measures cover adoption by military organisations, legal reviews, senior-level oversight of high-consequence applications, minimising unintended bias, appropriate care, transparent and auditable methods, training against automation bias, well-defined uses, rigorous testing and assurance across the life cycle, and safeguards such as deactivating systems that behave unexpectedly.
updates.notes: The text holds ten measures (A to J) for the development, deployment and use of military AI capabilities. Endorsing states undertake to implement the measures, make their commitment public and release information on implementation, support other efforts for responsible and lawful use, continue discussions among themselves, refine the measures or add new ones, and engage the rest of the international community, without prejudice to discussions in other fora. The declaration defines AI as the ability of machines to perform tasks that would otherwise require human intelligence, and autonomy as a spectrum involving a system operating without further human intervention after activation.

updates.issuing_body: Government representatives at the 2023 REAIM summit on responsible AI in the military domain, The Hague, organised by the Netherlands' Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Defence and co-hosted by the Republic of Korea
updates.summary: Joint call agreed by government representatives at the 2023 REAIM summit in The Hague on the responsible development, deployment and use of AI in the military domain. It names concerns about unreliable AI systems, human involvement, unclear liability and unintended escalation; commits to keeping humans responsible and accountable for decisions; stresses appropriate safeguards and human oversight, risk assessment and data governance consistent with international law; warns that adoption without sufficient research, testing and assurance may cause inadvertent harm; and invites states to develop national frameworks.
updates.notes: Agreed at the first REAIM summit, held at the World Forum in The Hague on 15-16 February 2023, organised by the Dutch foreign and defence ministries and co-hosted by South Korea, with some 2,000 delegates. The text has 25 numbered paragraphs: sixteen on shared understandings of the opportunities and risks of military AI, followed by the call to action proper (paragraphs 17 to 25), which asks states, the private sector, academia and civil society to build knowledge, exchange good practices and continue a multi-stakeholder dialogue, and ends by inviting all stakeholders worldwide to join it. The government's list of endorsing countries and territories (published 4 April 2025) names 58, among them China, the United States, the Netherlands and the Republic of Korea. The summit also announced a Global Commission on AI in the military domain. Later REAIM summits produced the Blueprint for Action (Seoul, 2024; INT-16) and the 2026 Pathways to Action (INT-18), which builds on both.

updates.summary: Agreement signed in Shanghai on 16 July 2026 by representatives of 29 countries, which became its founding members, establishing the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) as an independent intergovernmental international organisation headquartered in Shanghai. WAICO follows the purposes of the UN Charter and aims to promote international cooperation and global governance on AI and to ensure the healthy, orderly development of AI in a beneficial, safe and fair direction. It is to help bridge the AI divide by supporting Global South countries and is open to all countries.
updates.notes: Foreign Minister Wang Yi signed for China; the named signatories include Kazakhstan, Laos, Pakistan, Russia and Indonesia, and UN Secretary-General António Guterres attended the ceremony. The agreement remained open for signature until 31 July 2026; Georgia's ambassador signed it in Beijing on that day. The Chair's Statement of the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (17 July 2026) reports the signing, calls WAICO the world's first intergovernmental international organisation on AI, lists its guiding principles (the UN Charter, sovereignty and the diversity of civilisations, equality, multilateralism) and says it will maintain communication with other international organisations. China's Premier Li Qiang had announced the proposal to establish WAICO in July 2025, on the day the Global AI Governance Action Plan (CN-11) was released, with headquarters in Shanghai then under consideration.
updates.scope_note: A treaty creating an international organisation for AI cooperation and governance; safety content is the stated aim of safe, fair development rather than any rule. Include with a scope note.

verification.note: Stored and read in this run: the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs report on the signing ceremony (16 July 2026); the MFA's English text of the Chair's Statement of WAIC 2026 (17 July 2026); the MFA's text of Deputy Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu's remarks at the High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance (page updated 30 July 2025), which reports Premier Li Qiang's announcement of the WAICO proposal that morning; and the Embassy of Georgia in China's report of 31 July 2026 on Georgia's signature. updates.summary: Outcome document of the second summit on Responsible AI in the Military Domain (REAIM), held in Seoul on 9-10 September 2024 and co-organised by the Republic of Korea's foreign and defence ministries. Endorsed at the closing session and supported by 61 states, the declarative Blueprint lays out a roadmap for establishing norms for AI in the military domain. It suggests principles and a framework for future governance, emphasising that being responsible entails complying with international law, holding humans responsible and accountable, ensuring reliable and trustworthy AI, maintaining appropriate human involvement and improving explainability.
updates.notes: The Blueprint was endorsed at the closing session that followed the ministerial roundtable of 10 September 2024, which brought together government representatives from over 90 states. The summit's plenary sessions covered the implications of AI for international peace and security, including conflict dynamics and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, the responsible application of AI in the military domain, and its future governance. The 2026 REAIM Pathways to Action (INT-18) builds on the Blueprint, 'advanced at the REAIM Summit 2024 in Seoul', and on the 2023 Call to Action (INT-14).

updates.issuing_body: States adopting the outcome document of the third REAIM Summit (A Coruña, 4-5 February 2026), organised by Spain's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation and Ministry of Defence; 45 states on the summit page's list
updates.summary: Outcome document of the third REAIM summit (A Coruña, 4-5 February 2026), building on the 2023 Call to Action and the 2024 Blueprint for Action. Its 28 paragraphs invite states and other stakeholders to operationalise responsible military AI: compliance with humanitarian and human rights law, 'responsible by design', accountability of states and individuals without 'accountability gaps', AI assurance for reliability and security while anticipating AGI or ASI, and decision support that does not replace human judgement. National measures include pre-deployment risk assessments, TEVV, legal reviews, audit trails with incident reporting and a national focal point.
updates.notes: Known as the A Coruña Declaration; the Spanish summit page heads it 'Declaración de A Coruña: "REAIM 2026 - Camino para la acción"'. The summit was organised by Spain's foreign and defence ministries, with the Ministry for Digital Transformation and the city of A Coruña, and closed on 5 February 2026; more than 80 delegations of countries and international organisations took part. The summit page lists 45 endorsing states 'as of today' (Albania, Armenia, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Ecuador, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Ghana, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Kenya, Luxembourg, Malta, Morocco, Netherlands, Norway, Pakistan, Panama, Philippines, Portugal, Republic of Korea, Romania, Senegal, Singapore, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, Ukraine, United Kingdom); the United States and China are not on the list, and the document remains open to approval by other countries. Neither the document nor the pages give a day of adoption. The text notes UNGA resolutions 79/239 and 80/58, the Secretary-General's report A/80/78, the work of the CCW Group of Governmental Experts on lethal autonomous weapons systems and the Global Commission on REAIM's 'Responsible by Design' report. At international level it recommends voluntary confidence-building measures, including information sharing on national policies and legal-review methods, table-top exercises and crisis-communication arrangements.

updates.notes: The Friends Group was launched in May 2024 as a voluntary framework of countries supporting the spirit of the HAIP; as of March 2026 it had 66 countries and regions and 38 organisations in its Partners Community. The Tokyo meeting of 15-16 March 2026, hosted by Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications with the OECD and the World Bank as co-hosts, was attended by 34 Friends Group countries and regions, Brazil as an observer and 32 partner organisations. The plan is to be shared in coming international discussions. At the meeting the OECD announced a pilot version aimed at revising the HAIP Reporting Framework (OECD-02), and the World Bank announced an AI Academy to support capacity building in the Global South. The G7 Digital and Technology Ministers, meeting in Paris on 29 May under France's presidency, welcomed the Friends Group's initiatives and 'the related Action Plan announced in March 2026' (G7-04).

updates.issuing_body: Ministers and high-level authorities of Latin American and Caribbean countries at the Second Ministerial and High-Level Authorities Summit on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in Latin America and the Caribbean, Montevideo (organised by Uruguay's AGESIC with UNESCO and CAF)
updates.notes: Follow-up to the Santiago Declaration of October 2023 (INT-12), in line with the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI; it also highlights the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology and CAF's practical guide on designing AI public policies. The declaration and its roadmap were approved at the summit's closed session on 4 October 2024 with representatives of Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Cuba, Curaçao, Ecuador, El Salvador, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, the Dominican Republic and Uruguay; Bolivia and Dominica adhered later (update as of 1 December 2024), and Antigua and Barbuda (update as of 1 September 2025). The roadmap (version of 2 October 2024) calls for clear responsibilities among actors in the AI ecosystem and plans a methodology for designing AI regulatory proposals, annual reports on the use of UNESCO's readiness and ethical impact assessment tools, a regional study on racism and discrimination in AI used for public security, and guidelines on data governance for algorithm training, over a 12-month horizon with half-yearly follow-up. Chile handed leadership of the Working Group to Uruguay. The third summit, held in Santo Domingo on 25-26 June 2026, approved the Declaration of Santo Domingo and a 2026-2027 roadmap.
updates.original_title: Declaración de Montevideo: Para la construcción de un enfoque regional sobre la gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial y sus impactos en nuestra sociedad
updates.summary: Ministerial declaration adopted at the second regional summit on AI ethics (Montevideo, 3-4 October 2024) that reaffirms human-rights-centred AI governance, promotes international cooperation to maximise AI's benefits and mitigate its risks, and approves the Roadmap for Ethical AI for Latin America and the Caribbean 2024-2025. The roadmap's five areas are governance and regulation (including a mechanism against AI-amplified disinformation), talent and the future of work, protection of vulnerable groups, environment and climate change, and infrastructure. The declaration consolidates the regional Working Group on AI Ethics as a permanent dialogue body and makes the ministerial summit annual.
